summary: Proposes running ISO transport service (TSAP) on top of TCP so that ISO and CCITT session, presentation and application services can be used in the ARPA Internet without disrupting existing facilities. Hosts choosing to offer these services were expected to follow it. It was replaced by RFC 1006.

plainLanguage.summary: A new kind of mail system wanted to travel on the old roads. This memo explains how to put its envelopes inside the trucks the Internet already uses.

subtitle: Running ISO transport protocols on top of TCP to enable ISO applications on the Internet.

tldr.problem: ISO and CCITT have defined transport and higher-layer protocols (session, presentation, application), but the Internet uses TCP/IP. There is no way for ISO applications to run on the Internet without breaking TCP/IP implementations.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how to implement the ISO Transport Service Access Point (TSAP) using TCP as the underlying service, so that ISO layer 4 and above can operate unchanged on top of a TCP/IP network.
tldr.outcome: Organizations could begin migrating to ISO protocols without replacing their Internet infrastructure. The approach allowed development and deployment of ISO applications as a bridge strategy before ISO protocols matured. RFC 1006 later superseded it with an improved design.

facts.label: Connections for expedited data
facts.value: Two TCP connections (one regular, one for expedited)

today: RFC 983 was succeeded by RFC 1006, which provided improvements to the protocol design. Today, ISO protocols have largely been superseded by Internet protocols. However, the translation layer concept pioneered in this RFC—implementing a higher-layer service on top of a different lower-layer transport—remains a useful pattern for protocol adaptation.

sections.title: The ISO Protocol Stack
sections.content:
ISO and CCITT have defined a complete stack of protocols for Open Systems Interconnection (OSI). These include transport, session, presentation and application protocols. The ARPA Internet, by contrast, has TCP/IP. Both are layered protocol systems—the principle of layer independence means that if a lower layer provides the same service, higher layers do not need to know which lower layer implementation exists.

This RFC uses that principle: it defines a Transport Service Access Point (TSAP) that presents the ISO transport service to higher layers, but implements that service using TCP/IP underneath. Higher-layer ISO protocols (session, presentation, application) communicate through the TSAP without knowing it runs on TCP. This allows development and deployment of ISO applications in the TCP/IP Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISO world has a library of services and protocols they use. The Internet has a different library. By making a translator that turns ISO's service requests into Internet requests, we can use ISO applications on the Internet.

sections.title: Why This Transition Strategy
sections.content:
Two problems drove this design. First, ISO transport and network protocols were still being developed and were not yet stable. But higher-level ISO services (session, presentation, application) were ready to use. The RFC needed a medium to develop and test those higher layers. Since TCP/IP is mature and stable, TCP became that medium.

Second, a direct gateway between TCP and ISO at the network or transport layer would burden every Internet host with implementing two full transport stacks. Instead, the RFC chose to gateway exactly at the transport service access point, the boundary between transport and session. This way, only hosts that want to run ISO applications need the translation layer; the rest of the Internet is unaffected. The translation layer is also a natural boundary for a migration strategy: as ISO protocols mature, hosts can gradually shift from this gateway to native ISO protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: ISO's high-level services are ready but ISO's low-level plumbing is not. Instead of making everyone learn ISO's plumbing, we make a translator just for the high-level services, using TCP as the plumbing underneath.

sections.title: The TSAP Protocol Overview
sections.content:
The protocol (version 1) encapsulates ISO Transport Protocol Data Units (TPDUs) in TCP packets using a simple wrapper called a TPKT (TSAP Packet). A TPKT consists of a 4-byte header (version, reserved byte, and 16-bit packet length) followed by a pseudo-TPDU based on ISO transport format.

The protocol reserves TCP port 102 as the well-known port for ISO Transport Services. When an ISO application wants to connect, the TS-peer (an entity implementing this RFC's protocol) sends a connection request TPKT (code CR) with client and server identifiers. The server responds with a connection confirm TPKT (code CC) or disconnect (code DR) if the connection fails. After confirmation, both sides enter a symmetric peer state where either side can send data (DT), expedited data (ED), or disconnect requests.

The RFC uses a second TCP connection for expedited data, rather than TCP's urgent mechanism. This simplifies implementations by avoiding complex buffering and signal handling.
sections.plainLanguage: We wrap ISO messages in a simple envelope with a size field, send them over TCP port 102, and add a second TCP connection just for urgent messages. The protocol is like a conversation: first you agree to talk, then you exchange data, then you say goodbye.

sections.title: Connection States and Transitions
sections.content:
The protocol defines states for servers and clients. A server starts by listening on TCP port 102 (state S0). When a client connects and sends CR, the server moves to state S2, fires a T-CONNECT.INDICATION to its TS-user (the ISO session layer), and waits for the user's response. If the user accepts (T-CONNECT.RESPONSE), the server moves to the peer state (P0) and sends a CC TPKT. If the user rejects, the server sends DR and returns to listening.

A client starts in state C0. When the TS-user issues T-CONNECT.REQUEST, the client opens TCP port 102, sends a CR TPKT, and waits for a response (state C2). If a CC arrives, the client fires T-CONNECT.CONFIRMATION and enters the peer state. Once both sides reach the peer state P0, the protocol is completely symmetric: either side can send data, request expedited data, or disconnect.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sits at the door waiting for clients. When a client shows up, the server checks if anyone inside wants to talk to them. If yes, they shake hands and start talking. Either one can end the conversation.

sections.title: TPKT Structure and Parameters
sections.content:
The TPKT header is simple: an 8-bit version field (always 1 in this RFC), an 8-bit reserved field (must be zero), and a 16-bit packet length field specifying the total length in octets, including the header.

The pseudo-TPDU that follows is based on ISO transport format. For connection request (CR) and connection confirm (CC) TPDUs, the format includes an 8-bit header length, a 4-bit code, and a 4-bit credit field (always zero). The source and destination reference fields are ignored. The TSAP ID parameters in the variable data identify the client and server. An additional options parameter indicates whether expedited data is requested. For disconnect request (DR) TPDUs, a reason field specifies why the connection is closing. For data (DT) and expedited data (ED) TPDUs, a TPDU number and end-of-transmission flag are present (always zero). User data follows in all cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has a small label (is it a connection request, data, disconnect?) and metadata (who is talking to whom, how big is the message). The actual message data comes at the end.

sections.title: Implementation and Evolution
sections.content:
The RFC notes that a prototype implementation exists for 4.2BSD UNIX. The design uses a daemon that listens on TCP port 102, consults a database of registered ISO services when a connection request arrives, and spawns a child process to handle the connection. Libraries are provided so that programs implementing ISO services can easily use the TS-peer API.

The RFC explicitly acknowledges limitations in version 1. Quality of Service (QOS) parameters from ISO transport are not supported—they are left for version 2. The TSAP ID space is isolated from the TCP port space, using the TSAP port numbers defined in an appendix. Future versions of this standard are expected to change as both ISO and the migration strategy evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: An example implementation runs a helper program at port 102 that listens for connection requests and starts the right ISO service for each one. The design is simple enough to build quickly but is expected to improve as experience grows.
